config.title: OAuth2 PKCE Flow in a SPA

intro.title: OAuth2 PKCE Flow in a SPA
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular Single Page Application (SPA) that securely authenticates users using the OAuth2 Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) flow. You will learn the core concept of OAuth2 authorization, which allows your app to request limited access to a user's data on another service without handling their password directly. The main technologies involved are Angular for the frontend framework, TypeScript for type-safe code, and the Angular HTTP client to communicate with an OAuth2 authorization server. By the end, you'll understand how to generate a code verifier and challenge, redirect users for login, and exchange an authorization code for an access token securely.
intro.usecase: The OAuth2 PKCE flow is essential for securing single-page applications that integrate with third-party services like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub. Developers implement this pattern when building dashboards that display authenticated user data, such as project management tools that sync with external APIs. For example, a financial analytics SPA might use PKCE to securely obtain tokens for accessing banking APIs, then display personalized charts and transaction panels. This flow ensures that sensitive user data remains protected while enabling seamless, interactive experiences in modern web applications.

objectives: Implement the PKCE code verifier and challenge generation in an Angular service
Configure Angular routing to handle OAuth2 authorization code redirects
Construct HTTP requests to the authorization server with required PKCE parameters
Integrate token exchange logic to swap authorization codes for access tokens
Initialize and manage authentication state using Angular services
Apply route guards to protect application routes based on authentication status
Manipulate HTTP interceptors to attach access tokens to outgoing API requests

steps.title: Create OAuth configuration interface
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named OAuthConfig with the following properties: clientId (string), authEndpoint (string), tokenEndpoint (string), redirectUri (string), and scopes (string array).
steps.hint: Define an interface using the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.seedCode:
// app.module.ts - Add your imports here

// Create your OAuthConfig interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a properly defined OAuthConfig interface with all required properties and their types.
successCriteria: The OAuthConfig interface exists with clientId (string), authEndpoint (string), tokenEndpoint (string), redirectUri (string), and scopes (string[]) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the OAuthConfig interface with all required properties and proper TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an interface, but some properties are missing or have incorrect types. Make sure to include clientId, authEndpoint, tokenEndpoint, redirectUri, and scopes with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The OAuthConfig interface is not properly defined. You need to create an interface with the specified properties and their TypeScript types.

steps.title: Create OAuth service with configuration
steps.instruction: Create an Angular service class named OAuthService with a private config property of type OAuthConfig and initialize it with sample values in the constructor.
steps.hint: Use the @Injectable decorator to make it an Angular service. Define a private property 'config' with the OAuthConfig type and assign it in the constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: An OAuthService class is created with a private config property properly typed and initialized.
successCriteria: The OAuthService class is defined with @Injectable decorator, has a private config property of type OAuthConfig, and initializes it with sample values in the constructor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the OAuthService with proper configuration setup.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have: 1) @Injectable decorator, 2) private config property with OAuthConfig type, 3) constructor initialization with sample values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The service isn't properly set up. Review the requirements: create an Angular service class with private config property and initialize it.

steps.title: Add PKCE code verifier generation method
steps.instruction: In your OAuthService class, add a method named generateCodeVerifier that returns a secure random string.
steps.hint: You can use the crypto API to generate random bytes and convert them to a base64url-encoded string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The OAuthService class now has a generateCodeVerifier method that creates a secure random string for PKCE.
successCriteria: The generateCodeVerifier method is defined in OAuthService and returns a string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the PKCE code verifier generation method. This secure random string will be used to create the code challenge.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the method is named generateCodeVerifier and returns a string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Check that you've added generateCodeVerifier to OAuthService with a string return type.

steps.title: Add PKCE code challenge generation method
steps.instruction: In your OAuthService class, add a method named generateCodeChallenge that takes a codeVerifier string parameter and returns a Promise<string>. This method will compute the SHA-256 hash of the verifier and return it as a base64url-encoded string.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the Web Crypto API's crypto.subtle.digest method to compute the SHA-256 hash. Convert the verifier to a Uint8Array, hash it, then convert the result to base64url format.
steps.expectedOutcome: The OAuthService now has a generateCodeChallenge method that can create PKCE code challenges from verifiers using SHA-256 hashing.
successCriteria: The OAuthService contains an async generateCodeChallenge method that accepts a codeVerifier parameter and returns a Promise<string> with the base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the PKCE code challenge generation method. This is a critical part of the OAuth2 PKCE flow for SPAs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your method is async, uses SHA-256 hashing, and returns the result in base64url format (with + replaced by -, / replaced by _, and = padding removed).
steps.feedbackWrong: The method doesn't seem to be implemented correctly. Check that you're using the Web Crypto API for SHA-256 hashing and converting the result to base64url format.

steps.title: Initialize PKCE state in OAuth service
steps.instruction: In your OAuthService class, add two private properties: codeVerifier and codeChallenge, both initialized to null and typed as string | null.
steps.hint: Use TypeScript's private modifier and type annotations. These properties will store the PKCE state temporarily.
steps.expectedOutcome: The OAuthService will have private properties to store the PKCE code verifier and challenge, ready for use in later steps.
successCriteria: OAuthService contains private properties codeVerifier and codeChallenge, both typed as string | null and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the PKCE state properties to your service. These will be used to store the code verifier and challenge during the OAuth flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both properties are private, typed as string | null, and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The properties are missing or incorrectly defined. They should be private, typed as string | null, and initialized to null.

steps.title: Create authorization URL builder method
steps.instruction: In your OAuthService class, add a public method named buildAuthUrl that returns a string containing the complete OAuth2 authorization URL with PKCE parameters.
steps.hint: Construct the URL by combining the authorization endpoint from your config with query parameters like client_id, redirect_uri, response_type, scope, code_challenge, and code_challenge_method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The OAuthService now has a buildAuthUrl method that constructs the authorization URL with all required PKCE parameters.
successCriteria: The buildAuthUrl method exists in OAuthService, returns a string URL, and includes PKCE parameters (code_challenge and code_challenge_method).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the authorization URL builder method with proper PKCE parameters.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but it might be missing some required PKCE parameters or not returning a complete URL. Check that you include code_challenge and code_challenge_method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buildAuthUrl method is not present or doesn't return a proper authorization URL with PKCE parameters.

steps.title: Add component state for authorization URL
steps.instruction: In your AppComponent class, add a public property named 'authUrl' with type 'string' to store the generated authorization URL.
steps.hint: Declare the property inside the AppComponent class body, similar to how you'd add any class property in TypeScript.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent will have a property ready to hold the authorization URL string that will be generated later in the OAuth flow.
successCriteria: AppComponent has a public 'authUrl' property declared with type 'string'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the authUrl property to store the authorization URL. This will be essential for managing the OAuth flow state in your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the property is declared as 'public authUrl: string' inside the AppComponent class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The authUrl property wasn't properly added. Remember to declare it as a public string property within the AppComponent class.

steps.title: Implement initialization to generate PKCE values
steps.instruction: In your AppComponent class, implement the ngOnInit() lifecycle hook to generate the code verifier, code challenge, and build the authorization URL using your OAuthService methods.
steps.hint: Remember to call the generateCodeVerifier(), generateCodeChallenge(), and buildAuthUrl() methods from your OAuthService instance and assign the result to your authUrl property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent will now automatically generate PKCE values and build the authorization URL when the component initializes.
successCriteria: AppComponent implements OnInit with ngOnInit() method that calls OAuthService methods to generate code verifier, code challenge, and build authUrl.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the ngOnInit lifecycle hook to initialize PKCE values. This ensures the authorization URL is ready when your component loads.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling all three methods: generateCodeVerifier(), generateCodeChallenge(), and buildAuthUrl(). Also ensure you're assigning the result to the authUrl property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnInit method isn't properly implemented. Remember to implement the OnInit interface and add the ngOnInit() method that calls the OAuthService methods to generate PKCE values.

steps.title: Create basic component template structure
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent's template, add a container div with a heading and paragraph explaining the OAuth PKCE flow.
steps.hint: Use the template property in the @Component decorator to add HTML structure. Include a div, an h1 heading, and a p paragraph.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent template will have a div container with a heading and paragraph describing the OAuth PKCE flow.
successCriteria: The template contains a div element with an h1 heading and a p paragraph with OAuth PKCE flow explanation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the basic UI structure for the OAuth authorization flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've included all required elements: a div container, h1 heading, and p paragraph.

steps.title: Add authorization button with OAuth URL
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent template, add a button element with a click handler that redirects to the authUrl using window.location.href.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click) to call a method that performs the redirect.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Button with click handler
<button (click)="redirectToAuth()">Login with OAuth</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a functional button that initiates the OAuth2 PKCE flow when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element is added to the template with (click) event binding that calls redirectToAuth method, which uses window.location.href to redirect to authUrl.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the authorization button that will redirect users to the OAuth provider.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the correct click handler and redirect logic using window.location.href.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or redirect logic is missing. Review the step instructions carefully.
